UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company                     )
                                                              )
           v.                                                 )                     Docket No. EL26-38-000
                                                              )
Midcontinent Independent System Operator Inc.                 )

                        NOTICE OF INTERVENTION AND COMMENTS OF
                          THE ORGANIZATION OF MISO STATES, INC.

           The Organization of MISO States, Inc. (“OMS”) submits the following Notice of

Intervention and Comments in response to a complaint filed by Southern Indiana Gas and Electric

Company d/b/a CenterPoint Energy Indiana South (“SIGECO”) against the Midcontinent

Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

(“Commission”) in the above-captioned proceeding. 1 In the Complaint, SIGECO requests that the

Commission order MISO to establish a rate schedule under its Open Access Transmission, Energy,

and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) that would provide a mechanism for SIGECO to

recover all costs associated with SIGECO’s compliance with a recent order from the U.S. Secretary

of Energy (“Secretary”). 2

           OMS agrees with SIGECO that MISO’s Tariff lacks a mechanism to enable cost recovery

pursuant to the DOE Order and a mechanism is needed for SIGECO to recover prudently incurred

costs. However, the Secretary’s issuance of the DOE Order due to a self-determined energy

emergency does not obviate the Commission’s obligation to establish just and reasonable rates.

Given the relatively novel nature of the Complaint and the underlying DOE Order as well as the


1
    Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Co. v. MISO, Docket No. EL26-38-000 (filed Jan. 5, 2026) (“Complaint”).
2
  U.S. Department of Energy, Order No. 202-25-13 (issued Dec. 23, 2025) (the “DOE Order”). The DOE Order was
issued to CenterPoint Energy, Inc. regarding F.B. Culley Generating Station – Unit 2. SIGECO is the operating
utility subsidiary of CenterPoint Energy, Inc. and owns and operates Unit 2 of the F.B. Culley Generating Station.

                                                         1
 critical role of states in determining the appropriate method for allocating utility-incurred costs,

OMS urges the Commission to direct MISO to engage with MISO states in determining any cost

recovery or cost allocation methodologies for the costs incurred by SIGECO attributable to the

DOE Order. In the alternative, OMS request that the Commission set this Complaint for a hearing

pursuant to section 206(g)(3) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”). 3 In either case, OMS stresses that

any ultimate cost assignment that results from this proceeding should be based on a clear

demonstration of need and commensurate with benefits received to help mitigate unintended

consequences.

    I.     NOTICE OF INTERVENTION

           OMS is a non-profit, self-governing organization comprised of representatives from the

seventeen regulatory bodies with jurisdiction over entities participating in MISO and serves as the

regional state committee for the MISO region. OMS coordinates regulatory oversight among its

members, makes recommendations to MISO, the MISO Board of Directors, the Commission, and

other relevant government entities and intervenes in proceedings before the Commission to express

the positions of OMS members. As such, OMS files its Notice of Intervention in this proceeding

under Rule 214(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure. 4

           Service of pleadings, documents, and communications in this proceeding should be made

on the following:

     II.   COMMENTS

          In the DOE Order, the Secretary determined that the continued operation of Unit 2 of

SIGECO’s F.B. Culley Generating Station (“Culley Unit 2”) beyond its planned retirement date

“is necessary to best meet the emergency arising from increased demand, determined shortage,

and other causes, and serve the public interest under FPA section 202(c).” 5 DOE’s use of section

202(c) to keep Culley Unit 2 operating past its planned December 2025 retirement raises critical

questions relevant to all MISO states. 6 SIGECO’s request that the Commission direct MISO to

create a cost recovery and allocation mechanism pursuant to the DOE Order should only proceed

with rigorous review and an opportunity for meaningful engagement from MISO states.

          States have long held primary authority over resource adequacy, generation siting, and

utility investment decisions consistent with the FPA’s foundational federal-state framework. While

the Commission regulates wholesale markets and interstate transmission, states are responsible for

determining what generation is needed, where it is located, how it is financed, and whether it is

prudent to serve retail customers. This jurisdictional boundary ensures that decisions about cost,

environmental impact, and community needs remain accountable to the state regulators most

directly responsible for customer protection and affordability. DOE’s invocation of emergency

authority under section 202(c) does not displace this state role.

          A.          The Commission Should Ensure Meaningful Engagement with the States in
                      Any Determination on Cost Recovery or Cost Allocation Methodologies.

          OMS respectfully requests that the Commission direct MISO to engage with its member

states and stakeholders to determine any cost recovery or cost allocation methodologies associated

with Culley Unit 2. Advancing cost allocation decisions without such engagement undermines the


5
    DOE Order at 5.
6
    DOE Order at 2.

                                                  3
 longstanding and critical role of states in resource adequacy and cost responsibility under the FPA

and as participants in MISO. Any allocation of costs must adhere to fundamental cost-causation

and beneficiary-pays principles and ensure that customers are not required to bear costs from which

they do not cause or benefit, respectively. 7 States must have a meaningful opportunity to evaluate

impacts to their ratepayers and to represent those interests before the Commission reaches any

final determination in the instant case.

        Under the FPA, the Commission may resolve a complaint through alternative dispute

resolution procedures, by issuing an order on the merits based upon the pleadings, or by setting

the matter for hearing. 8 OMS respectfully requests that the Commission direct MISO to initiate a

stakeholder process to evaluate appropriate cost allocation and recovery approaches related to

SIGECO’s compliance with the DOE Order. Alternatively, if the Commission grants the Complaint

and determines that it should be fully resolved in this proceeding, OMS requests that the

Commission exercise its authority to establish hearing procedures to determine the justness and

reasonableness of any proposed cost recovery and cost allocation mechanisms, including expected

rate impacts. Such procedures should provide affected states, customers, and stakeholders an

opportunity to comment thereby ensuring transparency, due process, and fairness before any costs

are shifted to ratepayers as a result of the DOE Order.

        Thorough discussion and careful consideration are essential before assigning cost

responsibility for the emergency operation of Culley Unit 2. Any cost allocation framework

adopted in this proceeding must be both equitable and durable, particularly given the likelihood




7
  Constellation Mystic Power, LLC v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1028, 1051 (D.C. Cir., 2022); Pub. Serv. Comm’n of
  Wisconsin, 150 FERC ¶ 61,104, 61,704 (2015) (“SSR cost allocation should be commensurate with reliability
  benefits received from continued operation of an SSR Unit”).
8
  18 C.F.R. § 385.206(g) (2025).

                                                       4
 that DOE continues to issue section 202(c) orders extending the operation of other aging thermal

units in the MISO region. 9

           Under SIGECO’s proposal, costs would be broadly allocated across MISO’s North and

Central Subregions, including to customers and states for which no reliability benefit has been

identified, including Indiana. By contrast, a similar situation arose in PJM following the

Secretary’s issuance of a section 202(c) order for the Eddystone Generating Station on May 30,

2025. 10 In that instance, PJM, its member states, and other stakeholders initiated a Critical Issue

Fast Path process to develop a just and reasonable cost recovery mechanism under the PJM Tariff. 11

That stakeholder-driven approach underscores a fundamental principle: meaningful engagement

and transparent deliberation are essential before costs are imposed on customers, particularly

where benefits are unclear or have not been demonstrated.

           B.       The Commission Should Ensure Any Cost Allocation Is Based Upon a Clear
                    Need and Demonstratable Benefits.

           A foundational principle of ratemaking is that costs must be roughly commensurate with

benefits. To satisfy the “just and reasonable” standard required by law, any cost allocation

methodology must demonstrate a clear nexus between the costs incurred and the benefits received.

In evaluating whether such a relationship exists, material differences among states and regions

must be considered, including variations in load forecasts, resource mix, retirement schedules, and

system conditions. These differences directly affect whether, where, and to what extent a reliability

    U.S. DOE, Order No. 202-25-9 (issued Nov. 18, 2025); U.S. DOE, Order No. 202-25-12 (issued Dec. 23, 2025), all
    available at: https://www.energy.gov/ceser/2025-doe-202c-orders (last accessed Jan. 20, 2026).

     U.S. DOE, Order No. 202-25-4 (issued May 30, 2025).
11

    https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/task-forces/202cstf/postings/202cstf-issue-charge.pdf.

                                                           5
 or economic benefit is realized and, therefore, must inform any determination of cost responsibility

and cost allocation.

            Pursuant to the requirements of sections 202(c), 306, and 309 of the FPA and basic

ratemaking principles, the Commission should require evidence of need, benefit, and

proportionality before authorizing any rate recovery mechanism requested by the Complaint. Any

such recovery must also include a detailed explanation of why existing MISO planning and cost

allocation frameworks – designed precisely for evaluating regional needs and benefits – were

inadequate or not followed. Additionally, robust and routine transparency regarding the operations

and related costs of plants issued 202(c) orders is critical in providing states visibility into costs

that could be passed onto ratepayers. MISO has already been directed to share information about

the operational availability of Culley Unit 2 with DOE, and sharing this data with related market

impacts, even as a broad overview, would help inform state regulators on costs to operate affected

units. 12

            In short, absent a clearly substantiated need and benefit – to the extent a need and benefit

exist – and a sound planning foundation, there is no legal or procedural basis, other than the DOE

Order, for assigning these costs to any ratepayer. 13 Ongoing reforms including MISO’s ERAS

initiative, interconnection queue reform, continued progress on long-range transmission planning,

and other reforms demonstrate that the MISO region is actively enabling the development of new

 generation resources to meet future system needs without resorting to ad hoc or unsupported cost

recovery and allocation mechanisms.

       C.      A Comprehensive Stakeholder Process and a Thoroughly Vetted Cost
               Allocation Method Will Help Prevent Unintended Consequences.

       Absent a comprehensive stakeholder process and a carefully vetted cost allocation

framework, overly broad, premature, or unsupported cost recovery determinations risk significant

unintended consequences. Approving an expansive, unduly broad cost allocation mechanism for

section 202(c)-related costs could encourage a “race to the bottom,” where selection of units for

emergency operation is driven less by system need and more by the ability to socialize costs across

the MISO region. Such outcomes would undermine disciplined planning and distort decision-

making at both the utility and state regulator levels.

       If the Commission routinely approves broad regional cost allocation for 202(c) order costs

without a demonstrated, commensurate benefit, utilities may be incentivized to accelerate

retirements and cash in on a 202(c) order cost shift, moving costs away from local customers and

onto an 11-state region. Relying on an arbitrary regional cost allocation may shield utilities and

states from the political and economic consequences of local resource decisions, create perverse

incentives to prolong emergency operations, distort market signals, and increase reliance on

section 202(c) orders as a substitute. OMS recognizes that the lack of a clear demonstration of

need in DOE’s 202(c) orders has put the Commission in a position of having to approve cost

allocation mechanisms where benefits may not exist or at best, are unclear. Unfortunately, this




                                                  7
 means traditional benefit calculations may not apply in this proceeding, leaving only the scope of

DOE’s self-determined emergency, as described in each individual 202(c) order, to assign costs. 14

           The Commission has an independent responsibility under the FPA to ensure that any rates,

terms, and conditions it approves are just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory. That

obligation includes ensuring that costs are prudently incurred and appropriately allocated based on

demonstrable benefits, rather than defaulting to broad regionalization for administrative

convenience. A robust stakeholder process – grounded in transparent analysis of alternatives, unit

selection, system need, and cost impacts – will help ensure that cost allocation decisions are

equitable and consistent with long-standing cost-causation and beneficiary pays principles, while

avoiding precedents that could distort future resource planning and emergency actions.

     III. CONCLUSION

           OMS submits this Notice of Intervention and Comments because a majority of OMS

members support this filing. 15 This should not be construed to mean that all OMS members agree

with all comments above. Individual OMS members reserve the right to file separate comments.

In recognition of such, the following members voted in support of this filing:

           Illinois Commerce Commission
           Iowa Utilities Commission
           Kentucky Public Service Commission
           Michigan Public Service Commission
           Minnesota Public Utilities Commission

           Montana Public Service Commission
